sources: CRA — Guide T4002, Chapter 4 (CCA) · current · when you sell depreciable property, the class is reduced by the lesser of (proceeds minus related expenses) and the capital cost; a negative column 7 means a recapture of CCA, added to income; additions in the same period count before the comparison; no CCA when column 7 is negative; terminal loss when no property is left and a positive balance remains

CRA — Completing Form T2125, column 7 (canada.ca, page details 2026-08-31) · current · UCC = start-of-year UCC + additions − proceeds of dispositions; negative = recapture, report on line 8230 Other income; positive with no property left = terminal loss, line 9270
B11 (this series) · 2026 · Class 50 laptop $2,000 written off 100% in 2026 (Income Tax Regs 1100(2), SC 2026 c. 3) → UCC $0
CRA T4127 (Jan 2026) and CPP 2026, via b4/calc.py · 2026 · tax + CPP for the B4 freelancer (MB, single, $60,000 net)

Calculation (not a CRA rule): b12/calc.py → data.json. UCC $0 − lesser of ($700 proceeds, $2,000 cost) = −$700 → recapture $700 → tax + CPP $248.94 at 2026 rates (35.6¢ per $1). Replacement $2,500 in the same year: $0 + $2,500 − $700 = $1,800 UCC, no recapture. Dependencies: the class balance at year end (other Class 50 property counts), selling costs, the year's rates and income, mixed business/personal use; a sale above the original cost also triggers a capital gain (not covered). Example only.

yt.description:
You wrote off the whole laptop. Then you sold it for $700. Here's the catch.

Example (continuing the last video): a $2,000 laptop claimed 100% as capital cost allowance (Class 50). Its tax value (undepreciated capital cost) is now $0.
• Sell it for $700: $0 − $700 = −$700. A negative balance at year end is a recapture of CCA, and it goes back into business income (Form T2125, line 8230).
• For a Manitoba freelancer netting $60,000, that's about $249 in tax + CPP (2026 rates).
• Fair, really: you deducted value the laptop never actually lost.

The fix: buy the replacement in the same year. Its cost goes into the class first: $0 + $2,500 − $700 = $1,800 still to claim, and no recapture.

Only 60% for work? Reply 60 and we'll run it.

Sources: CRA Guide T4002 ch. 4 (CCA, recapture, terminal loss); CRA Form T2125 column 7; CRA T4127 2026 rates, CPP 2026. Example only; general information, not tax advice.

_vo: You wrote off the whole laptop. Two years later, you sell it for seven hundred. Here's the catch. Last time: a two-thousand-dollar laptop, claimed one hundred percent. Its tax value is now zero. Sell it for seven hundred, and that zero goes negative: minus seven hundred. CRA calls that recapture. It goes straight back into your business income. For our Manitoba freelancer, that's about two hundred and fifty dollars in tax and CPP. Fair, really. You deducted value the laptop never actually lost. The fix: buy the replacement in the same year. Its cost goes into the class first. Twenty-five hundred new, minus seven hundred sold: eighteen hundred left to claim. No recapture. But what if the laptop is only sixty percent for work? Reply sixty, and we'll run it.
